conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any fevers, chills, or recent infections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers, but I’ve had some chills and nausea. No vomiting. Also, my eyes feel irritated—kind of gritty, and my vision is a bit blurry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had iritis before, right? That can happen with AS. I’ll get ophthalmology to check your eyes to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had it once before. That was much more painful. This feels milder, but I wanted to mention it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good call. We’ll get that checked. Your labs from the outside hospital showed elevated inflammation markers—CRP was 17 and ESR 83. Our repeat CRP is still high at 14.2, so there’s active inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely a flare? I was given 60 mg of prednisone at the other hospital and it helped a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks like an inflammatory flare. Rheumatology mentioned that AS doesn’t usually have ‘flares’ like this—more chronic stiffness—but your symptoms do match what you’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. The steroids usually help me get through it. I’d like to stay on them a bit longer if possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can do a short 10-day taper as you requested. But we also need to protect your stomach—especially since you didn’t tolerate ketorolac before due to GI discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, NSAIDs really bother my stomach. I stopped ibuprofen because of that and my allergy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you sucralfate and keep you on omeprazole to protect your stomach. We’ll also use ketorolac with caution and add acetaminophen for pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds okay. What about my regular pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on your OxyContin 50 mg twice daily and oxycodone as needed. We’ll also keep the lidocaine patch on the painful area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m just worried this won’t settle down quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your pain closely. You’re also on lisinopril for blood pressure, albuterol and Pulmicort for asthma, and CPAP for sleep apnea—all of which we’ll continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I use CPAP every night. My breathing’s okay now, just the pain makes it hard to take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll avoid anything that could worsen your stomach. Your urine culture showed mixed flora, but it’s likely contamination, and there’s no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about my eyes? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ophthalmology will see you tomorrow. Given your history, we want to rule out iritis, but your symptoms sound more like dry eyes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Ophthalmology saw you this morning. They didn’t find any signs of iritis—your eyes look normal. They think it’s dryness, especially with the AC on and your CPAP use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So no iritis this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, they were reassured. They recommend using preservative-free artificial tears as needed for comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that. How’s the back pain looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re moving better today. Your pain seems more controlled. Blood pressure is stable, and labs show CRP is still elevated but not worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit better. The steroids are helping, and the sucralfate seems to be protecting my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep you on the current plan. You’re improving, so we’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be good. What will I be going home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue OxyContin, oxycodone as needed, lidocaine patch, and your asthma and blood pressure meds. We’ll give you a short prednisone taper—20 mg daily for a few days, then down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, four times a day for stomach protection while you’re on NSAID-like meds. And acetaminophen every 8 hours for pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I see rheumatology again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we strongly recommend follow-up. They can help find a long-term solution that doesn’t rely so much on steroids, maybe a biologic agent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I’ve had bad reactions before—like infections. I’m hesitant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But it’s worth discussing alternatives. Steroids long-term can cause problems like bone loss, especially with your weight and other conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it and talk to my PCP. I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Your exam shows less tenderness in the SI joint, and you’re walking with your cane more comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you today. Continue all your home meds, the prednisone taper, sucralfate, and acetaminophen. Use the eye drops as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with my PCP and rheumatology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Call if pain worsens, or if eye symptoms return. Otherwise, keep managing at home and stay on CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for helping me get through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you're here for worsening flank pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's the same pain I’ve had before—left flank and low back. It started right after I tried to lower my prednisone dose last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were on a taper from 60 mg down to 40 mg, and then you adjusted it yourself between 20 and 50 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I was trying to wean off slowly, but the pain came back fast. Nothing else helps like prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’ll keep you on your current pain meds—OxyContin, lidocaine patch, and your other medications. We also gave you 50 mg of OxyContin when you arrived.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. But will I get prednisone again? It’s the only thing that really calms the flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to restart prednisone at 60 mg daily. But we want to taper it much more slowly this time—by 5 mg every three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. I think going too fast last time triggered this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also ordered blood tests and an X-ray of your spine to check for fractures or other issues, since you're on long-term steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had X-rays before. Do you think I have a fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unlikely, but steroids can weaken bones over time, so we want to be sure. No symptoms like fever, urinary issues, or numbness—just the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just the pain. I can walk fine, no tingling or bladder changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll monitor your labs and get the imaging results. For now, rest and stay on your CPAP at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, your blood work came back. White count is a bit high at 10.6, but that could be from inflammation or steroids. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal for me when I’m flaring?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, steroids can raise white counts, and inflammation from pain flares can too. Nothing concerning in your kidney or liver values.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your spine X-ray is back—no fractures or dislocations. Degenerative changes, but nothing acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a broken bone. Is it definitely my ankylosing spondylitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your rheumatologist mentioned that these frequent flares aren’t typical for AS. It’s more chronic and steady. But since steroids help, we’re treating it symptomatically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not textbook, but when I lower the dose, the pain comes back. It feels inflammatory.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hear you. That’s why we’re restarting the 60 mg and tapering slowly. We also consulted the chronic pain team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did they say?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They recommend adding a muscle relaxant—tizanidine twice daily—and using NSAIDs like Advil as needed, though you have a history of NSAID allergy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had reactions before, but maybe I can try a different one? Etodolac was mentioned last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start tizanidine and hold NSAIDs for now. We’re also adding calcium and vitamin D to protect your bones from long-term steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been on steroids for a while now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And because the taper is long, we’re prescribing Bactrim to prevent infections, especially since you’ve had issues before with biologics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want to go back on those. Too many side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look better—hemoglobin improved, and white count is up a bit but expected on steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your pain is more controlled, and you’re moving better. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What’s the plan after discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue the prednisone taper—60 mg daily, then down by 5 mg every three days. You’ll need to cut pills in half.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that. And the new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tizanidine twice daily for a week, calcium with vitamin D daily, and Bactrim daily for infection prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can still use Advil if needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold off on NSAIDs for now due to allergy risk. Use acetaminophen or your oxycodone for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you’re doing well. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Do I need to see rheumatology again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your preference not to restart biologics, we’re not scheduling rheumatology. But you’ll follow up with the chronic pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that works. And my partner is my healthcare proxy, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll send all instructions and prescriptions to your pharmacy. Rest, stay on CPAP, and call if pain worsens or you develop fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate the slow taper plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you're here for severe back pain. Can you tell me more about what’s going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. The pain started last night—left flank and lower back, right around my SI joint. It’s 10 out of 10, just like my usual flares. I can’t move without it getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before. Is it the same kind of pain you’ve had during past ankylosing spondylitis flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly the same. It wakes me up at night, it’s worse with movement, and nothing helps except prednisone and my pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER, you got some hydromorphone and ketorolac. Are you feeling any relief from that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little, but it’s not enough. I need prednisone. It’s the only thing that really calms this down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ve reviewed your history. You’ve had several admissions this year for similar pain. But your labs show only mild inflammation—CRP is 12.4 and ESR is 38. Not extremely high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But that’s still elevated, right? And I know my body. This is inflammatory. I need steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted rheumatology. They don’t think this is a typical inflammatory flare of ankylosing spondylitis. AS usually doesn’t flare this often or this severely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had sacroiliitis on MRI before. And infliximab helped me the most. Why can’t I restart something like that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with infliximab, but you stopped because of infections. And you’ve had recurrent abscesses in the past. Before restarting any biologic, we need to make sure you’re not at high risk for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I can’t keep living like this. I need something that works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not dismissing your pain. The chronic pain team also saw you. They recommend continuing your current opioids and increasing tizanidine, or trying physical therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tizanidine makes me sleepy and sometimes worsens my spasms. And I don’t want physical therapy right now—it hurts too much to move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You also declined NSAIDs, which they recommended, because of past GI bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’ve had ulcers before. I can’t risk that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your home medications—oxycontin, oxycodone, lisinopril, albuterol, and tizanidine. We’re not changing your pain regimen during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re not giving me prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. The team feels it’s not clearly indicated, especially given your history of infections with immunosuppression. But we support your interest in discussing biologics again as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel like I’m being sent home without help. This pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is real, and we believe you. But our job is to balance relief with safety. We’ve repeated your hepatitis panel and TB test—quantiferon gold—to make sure you’re safe to start biologics later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can restart infliximab or something like it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a conversation for your rheumatologist. We recommend you call to schedule a follow-up. If tests come back clear, they may consider restarting a biologic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll call them. But what about now? I’m still in pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your scheduled oxycodone and oxycontin. We can also give breakthrough doses if needed. And we’ve increased your tizanidine to 4 mg twice daily as needed, but only if you feel it helps without worsening spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try it, but I’m not hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurting, but maybe a little better. The pain meds help a bit, but it’s still 8 out of 10.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. White count is down to 6.7, kidney function is normal. No signs of infection or organ stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it means your body isn’t fighting an infection or severe inflammation. We’re glad you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, can I ask—why did I have to be admitted if you’re not changing my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We admitted you to fully evaluate your pain, rule out serious causes like infection or fracture, and coordinate with specialists. We also wanted to ensure your safety with your complex history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess that makes sense. But it feels like I’m being discharged with the same pain I came in with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s frustrating. But we’ve set you up for next steps—rheumatology follow-up, continued pain management, and support from your PCP. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preparing for discharge. Your condition is stable. You’re alert, breathing well, and your vitals are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m going home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re sending you home with the same medications, including increased tizanidine if needed. Please follow up with rheumatology to discuss biologics once your TB test comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them. Thank you for listening, even if we didn’t agree on everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for being open with us. We care about your comfort and safety. Please reach out if things worsen. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you came in with trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been having a lot of shortness of breath. I can’t even walk up the stairs without stopping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when did this start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started after my Simponi infusion. I got chest tightness and a cough, like I’ve had before. Then seven days ago, I spiked a fever—up to 102.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what happened after the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The fever went away after two days with prednisone and azithromycin, but my cough and breathing got worse. I’m using my nebulizer six times a day and can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You were given albuterol and ceftriaxone in the ER. We’re admitting you because your asthma flare isn’t improving with outpatient treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had asthma for years, but this feels worse than usual. I use albuterol before exercise, but I don’t always use my other inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll help you get through this flare. Your chest X-ray didn’t show pneumonia, but there’s some mild atelectasis in the bases—likely from not being able to take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s an asthma exacerbation triggered by a recent upper respiratory infection. Your labs are mostly normal—white count is 8.9, no signs of severe infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had to stop past TNF inhibitors because of infections. I’m worried about Simponi.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear that concern. But your rheumatologist feels the benefits outweigh the risks, and your breathing has improved since restarting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I guess. What’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your prednisone at 60 mg daily, give you duoneb treatments every six hours, and monitor your breathing. You’re on room air with 94% oxygen, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on levofloxacin, but I didn’t want to continue it—side effects bother me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ve switched you to Augmentin for two more days to finish the antibiotic course, since you were already on azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s better. I’ve had bad reactions to other antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on that. For now, rest and let the nebulizers do their work. We’ll check on you regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. How are you feeling after your first night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I slept a bit more. The nebulizers are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your breathing sounds improved—less wheezing. We’ll keep up the duonebs and steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely two days. We want to make sure your breathing keeps improving before sending you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been in before for pain, but this is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this admission is for your asthma, not pain. We’ll continue your home pain meds—oxycontin and breakthrough oxycodone—as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using Toradol in the past for pain—can I have that if needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can use Toradol for breakthrough pain, yes. But you’re allergic to NSAIDs, so we’ll be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I forgot—NSAIDs, methadone, Lyrica, gabapentin. I’ve had bad reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted all your allergies. You’re safe here. Let’s focus on getting your lungs better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your breathing is much better. You’re speaking in full sentences, no distress, and your lungs are clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. I can breathe deeper now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll finish Augmentin for two more days and continue prednisone at 60 mg for two more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then you’ll taper the prednisone by 10 mg each day until it’s done. Keep using albuterol and ipratropium nebulizers as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular inhalers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Once this flare settles, go back to your usual budesonide and albuterol. Try to use them more consistently—they help prevent flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I’ll follow up with my PCP too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, keep using your CPAP for sleep apnea—it helps your breathing overall. And take omeprazole for your GERD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually do. I know they matter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re doing well. You can go home now. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if breathing worsens. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time getting up. Nurse will assist you with discharge paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep monitoring your breathing. If you need your nebulizer more than usual, don’t wait—seek care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And follow up with your PCP within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll schedule that today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of worsening back pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, thanks. I’ve had this squeezing kind of back pain that started a few days ago. It radiates down to my SI joints. It’s worse than my usual pain from ankylosing spondylitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been on your regular OxyContin and oxycodone, right? Has that helped at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I’ve been taking the oxycodone more often than prescribed, but it’s not touching this pain. I’ve also tried ibuprofen—no help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you had a respiratory infection recently—cough and shortness of breath. How’s your breathing now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I was on Augmentin for bronchitis, and my asthma flared a bit, but that’s improved. The cough’s still there, but it’s not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Your chest X-ray showed no pneumonia or other issues, and your oxygen levels are normal. So we’re focusing on the back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve had AS flares before, but this one came on faster and feels different—more pressure than sharp pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. In the ER, you got IV morphine and Dilaudid, but it didn’t help much. We’ll try a different approach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d prefer not to stay on IV opioids long-term. My rheumatologist said Simponi has helped in the past.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already on Simponi—good. That’s a biologic that helps with inflammation from AS. We’ll keep supporting that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, we’re going to try IV ketorolac, which is a strong anti-inflammatory. It might work better than opioids for this type of pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m willing to try it. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve checked. You’re on omeprazole, which protects your stomach, so it’s safe for short-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today? Did the ketorolac help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, yes. It took a few hours, but the pressure-like pain has eased. Still some discomfort, but closer to my baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll give another dose today and then transition you back to your home pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need more IV meds? I’d like to avoid increasing my opioid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if this trend continues. You’ll go back to your regular OxyContin and oxycodone PRN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Augmentin? I think I have a day or two left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the full 7-day course today. Your cough has improved, and there’s no fever or infection signs, so that’s on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried it might be pneumonia, but the X-ray was clear, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chest X-ray showed no pneumonia or acute issues. Heart is a bit enlarged, but that’s known. Lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my asthma? I’ve been using the nebs less, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, lungs are clear on exam. You can keep using albuterol and ipratropium PRN if needed. Pulmicort as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Pain still manageable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. Still tender when I move, but the crushing feeling is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We checked your labs this morning—white count and CRP are normal, so no sign of infection or high inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: CRP? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: C-reactive protein—it’s a marker of inflammation. Yours is 2.9, which is mild. Supports that this was a flare, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. So Simponi is helping, but flares can still happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It reduces frequency and severity, but you may still have episodes, especially with stress or illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious lately—could that make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, anxiety and stress can amplify pain. You’re on sertraline—that’s important to keep taking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I am. I just worry about relying too much on pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We recommend trying ketorolac or similar anti-inflammatories first during future flares, if safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’d like to discharge you this morning. Any questions before we go over the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—I continue all my regular meds, finish the antibiotics, and follow up with my rheumatologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep taking your Simponi, asthma meds, lisinopril for blood pressure, and the rest as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the back pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try tizanidine or ketorolac first. Call your rheumatologist. Only increase opioids if absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for helping me avoid another opioid increase.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send the discharge summary to your PCP and rheumatologist. Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll stay on top of my meds and follow-up.
